subject: The 1031 exchange — when it's a power move, when it's a tax tail wagging a dog
preheader: 45/180-day rules · QI fees · The 'replacement-property panic' that costs more than the deferred tax

marketSnapshot.headline: The 1031 exchange: when it works, when it doesn't
marketSnapshot.body: 1031 exchanges let you defer capital gains tax by rolling proceeds from a sold rental into a like-kind replacement property. It's one of the most powerful long-term wealth-building moves in real estate — and one of the most over-rushed. The 45-day identification window and 180-day close window create artificial deadlines that can trap investors into accepting mediocre replacement properties. The math: 1031 only wins if your replacement is a real deal, not a forced one.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: 1031 saves $19k · replacement deal must clear that bar
dealSpotter.body: Sold a property held 5 years, $80k of long-term capital gains + depreciation recapture. Taxable bill at 24% effective ~$19k. The 1031 defers all of it IF you can find a replacement property in 45 days that's worth pursuing on its own merits. Quality of replacement is the whole game. A 'mediocre' replacement that earns 1.5% less per year erases the $19k savings within 3-5 years.

dealSpotter.address: Example: rush to identify a property
dealSpotter.headlineNumber: Identified deal in week 6 · overpaid 8% · lost the deferral
dealSpotter.body: Common failure mode: investor sells, the 45-day clock starts, they're scrambling. They identify a deal in week 6 at full ask in a competitive market, pay 8% over what the property is worth, and the deferred-tax savings are eaten by the over-pay. The lesson: identify replacement candidates BEFORE you list the property you're selling. If you can't find good replacements in advance, don't sell.

dealSpotter.headlineNumber: $12k unrealized gain · QI fees + complexity eat it · pay tax
dealSpotter.body: Held a small property 3 years, $12k of capital gains. Taxable bill ~$2,400. QI fees + 1031 friction = $1,500-2,500. The math barely works even when you find a clean replacement, and you've added a 45-day deadline to your life. Below ~$25k of unrealized gain, just pay the tax and buy the next deal cleanly.

blogFeature.title: 1031 exchange basics: how to defer capital gains on rental property
blogFeature.excerpt: The 45-day / 180-day rules, qualified intermediary requirements, like-kind property definitions, and the friction costs most investors don't price in. If you're up 30%+ on a property you've held 5+ years, this is a real lever.

qa.question: When should I do a 1031, and when should I just take the tax hit?
qa.answer: Three conditions all need to be true for a 1031 to be the right move. (1) The unrealized gain is large enough to justify the friction — typically $25k+ of deferred tax. (2) You have real replacement candidates identified BEFORE you sell, not 'I'll find something in the 45-day window.' (3) The replacement property is genuinely as good or better than what you'd buy if you weren't on a deadline. If any of those three is false, pay the tax and move on. The most common mistake: investors so attached to 'defer the tax!' that they buy a mediocre replacement in week 6 of the 45-day window, overpay 5-10%, and end up worse off than if they'd just paid the original tax bill.
